sections.title: Devanagari: vowels, consonants and vowel signs
sections.summary: Hindi is written in Devanagari, an alphasyllabary: each consonant letter carries a built-in 'a' that is changed by vowel signs (mātrās) or cancelled by the virāma. This chapter gives you the vowels, the consonant grid, conjuncts, nasal marks and the nuqta so you can read every later example.

rules.title: Every consonant letter carries an inherent 'a'
rules.body: A bare consonant letter is read with a short 'a' after it: क is ka, म is ma, ल is la. So कमल is k-m-l plus two inherent vowels: kamal. In modern Hindi the inherent 'a' at the very end of a word is silent (कमल = kamal, not kamala), and it is also usually dropped in the middle of longer words (समझना samajhnā, not samajhanā).

rules.title: Independent vowel letters
rules.body: Vowels have full letters used at the start of a word or after another vowel: अ a, आ ā, इ i, ई ī, उ u, ऊ ū, ए e, ऐ ai, ओ o, औ au, plus ऋ (ṛi, only in Sanskrit loans like ऋषि ṛṣi). Long and short vowels are different sounds and different letters: दिन din 'day' versus दीन dīn 'poor'.

rules.title: Vowel signs (mātrās) attach to consonants
rules.body: After a consonant the vowel is written as a sign, not a full letter: का kā, कि ki, की kī, कु ku, कू kū, के ke, कै kai, को ko, कौ kau. Most signs sit after, above or below the consonant, but the short-i sign ि is written to the LEFT of the consonant although it is pronounced after it: किताब kitāb. The sign for the inherent 'a' is nothing at all.

rules.title: The consonant grid and aspiration
rules.body: Consonants are arranged by place of articulation, in rows of five: velar क ख ग घ ङ, palatal च छ ज झ ञ, retroflex ट ठ ड ढ ण, dental त थ द ध न, labial प फ ब भ म; then य र ल व, श ष स, ह. In each row the second and fourth letters are aspirated (a puff of air): क ka / ख kha, ग ga / घ gha, च cha / छ chha, ज ja / झ jha, प pa / फ pha, ब ba / भ bha. Aspiration changes meaning: काल kāl 'time' versus खाल khāl 'skin'.

rules.title: Retroflex versus dental t and d
rules.body: Hindi has two sets of t/d sounds. Retroflex ट ṭ, ठ ṭh, ड ḍ, ढ ḍh are made with the tongue tip curled back; dental त t, थ th, द d, ध dh are made with the tongue touching the teeth. English t and d are closer to the retroflex ones, so English loanwords use ट and ड (टमाटर ṭamāṭar, डॉक्टर ḍŏkṭar). Our romanization marks retroflex sounds with a dot below.

rules.title: Virāma kills the inherent vowel
rules.body: The small stroke ् under a consonant (virāma or halant) removes its inherent 'a': क् is just k. It appears at the end of some Sanskrit loanwords and in careful spelling of clusters, but its main job is to show that two consonants join with no vowel between them. In most Hindi words the final 'a' is simply left unpronounced without writing a virāma.

examples.en: the sound k alone, no vowel

rules.title: Conjunct consonants
rules.body: When two consonants come together with no vowel between them, they are written as one combined shape (a conjunct). Usually the first consonant loses its vertical stem and joins the second: स + त = स्त (नमस्ते namaste), क + य = क्य (क्या kyā), प + र = प्र (प्रेम prem). A few conjuncts have special shapes: क्ष kṣ, त्र tr, ज्ञ (pronounced gy in Hindi: ज्ञान gyān), द्ध ddh. A following र is written as a small hook: प्र pr, क्र kr.

rules.title: Nasal marks: anusvāra and candrabindu
rules.body: The dot above a letter (anusvāra ं) stands for a nasal consonant before the next consonant, matching its row: हिंदी = हिन्दी hindī, संगीत sangīt. The moon-and-dot (candrabindu ँ) nasalises the vowel itself, like French 'on': हाँ hān 'yes', माँ mān 'mother', हूँ hūn. When a vowel sign already fills the space above the line (as in हैं, नहीं), the plain dot is written instead of candrabindu. In romanization we write both nasals as n.

rules.title: The nuqta: a dot below for extra sounds
rules.body: A dot under a letter (nuqta) changes its sound. Two native Hindi sounds use it: ड़ ṛ (a flapped retroflex, as in लड़का laṛkā 'boy', बड़ा baṛā 'big') and ढ़ ṛh (पढ़ना paṛhnā 'to read'). Loanwords from Persian, Arabic and English use क़ q, ख़ kh (as in ख़ुश khush), ग़ ġ, ज़ z and फ़ f: ज़रूर zarūr, फ़िल्म film, सफ़ेद safed. In everyday writing the nuqta is often left out, so ज़रूर may appear as जरूर; the pronunciation is the same.

rules.title: Other signs and the headline
rules.body: Letters of a word hang from a continuous top line (śirorekhā); a gap in the line marks a word boundary. ऑ / ॉ writes the English 'o' of 'coffee': कॉफ़ी kŏfī, डॉक्टर ḍŏkṭar. The two dots ः (visarga) are rare and give a light h: दुःख duḥkh 'sorrow'. The danda । is the Hindi full stop; question marks and commas are as in English.

examples.en: I am fine. (ends with a danda)

exercises.q: Which letter is 'ka'?
exercises.explain: क is ka; ख is the aspirated kha, ग ga and घ gha.

exercises.q: The inherent vowel of a bare consonant letter such as म is
exercises.explain: Every bare consonant is read with a short a: म = ma.

exercises.q: The vowel sign for short i (ि) is written to the left of the consonant but pronounced after it.
exercises.explain: किताब is read kitāb: the ि sits before क but is spoken after it.

exercises.q: Write the word 'kitāb' (book) in Devanagari: ___
exercises.explain: क + ि (short i before the letter), ता, ब: किताब.

exercises.q: Which of these is a retroflex consonant?
exercises.explain: ट ṭ is retroflex (tongue curled back); त, द, न are dental.

exercises.en: the first five vowel letters in dictionary order: a ā i ī u

exercises.q: The sign ् (virāma) adds a long ā to the consonant.
exercises.explain: The virāma removes the inherent a; the long ā is written with ा.

exercises.q: Transliterate पानी (water) into Latin letters: ___
exercises.explain: पा = pā (long ā), नी = nī (long ī).

exercises.q: Which vowel sign turns क into कू (kū)?
exercises.explain: ू is the long ū sign; ु is short u, ो is o, ी is long ī.

exercises.q: ख and क represent exactly the same sound.
exercises.explain: ख is aspirated kha, spoken with a puff of air; the difference changes meaning (काल kāl vs खाल khāl).

exercises.q: Write 'ghar' (house) in Devanagari: ___
exercises.explain: घ is the aspirated gha, र is ra; the final inherent a is silent.

exercises.q: In हिन्दी, the shape न्द is
options: a conjunct: n + d with no vowel between
exercises.explain: न loses its stem and joins द because no vowel comes between them.

exercises.q: Which nuqta letter writes the sound z (as in zarūr)? ___
exercises.explain: ज ja with a dot below becomes ज़ za.

exercises.q: The dot under ड़ (as in लड़का) marks a native flapped sound, not a borrowed Persian one.
exercises.explain: ड़ ṛ and ढ़ ṛh are native Hindi sounds; क़ ख़ ग़ ज़ फ़ are for loanwords.

exercises.q: Which word contains a candrabindu (nasalised vowel)?
exercises.explain: हाँ hān has ँ over the ā; हिंदी uses the anusvāra dot for the n before d.

exercises.q: Transliterate लड़का (boy) into Latin letters: ___
exercises.explain: ल la, ड़ ṛ with no vowel (the inherent a is dropped inside the word), का kā.

exercises.q: In Hindi the final inherent a of धन्यवाद is silent, so the word is read as
exercises.explain: Final inherent a is not pronounced in Hindi; न्य is the conjunct ny.

exercises.q: The anusvāra in संगीत (sangīt) stands for a nasal consonant pronounced before the g.
exercises.explain: Before a consonant the dot is read as the nasal of that row: here ṅ/n before g.

exercises.q: Write 'namaste' in Devanagari (it uses the conjunct स्त): ___
exercises.explain: न म + स्त (s joined to t) + े: नमस्ते.

exercises.q: Which pair is two spellings of the same word?
exercises.explain: The anusvāra dot before द equals a written न; the other pairs differ in vowel length and meaning.

sections.title: Nouns and gender
sections.summary: Every Hindi noun is masculine or feminine, and the gender drives the endings of adjectives, possessives and verbs. Learn the -ā/-ī patterns, the main exceptions, and the plural of each noun class.

rules.title: Two genders, no neuter
rules.body: Every noun is either masculine (m.) or feminine (f.), including objects and ideas: घर ghar 'house' is m., किताब kitāb 'book' is f. The gender shows up on adjectives, possessives and verbs that go with the noun: अच्छा घर, अच्छी किताब. Learn each noun with its gender; the ending often, but not always, gives it away.

rules.title: Nouns in -ā are usually masculine
rules.body: Most nouns ending in -ā (-आ) are masculine: कमरा kamrā 'room', केला kelā 'banana', बेटा beṭā 'son', कपड़ा kapṛā 'cloth', दरवाज़ा darvāzā 'door'. Exceptions are mostly Sanskrit or Persian words: माता mātā 'mother', भाषा bhāṣā 'language', दवा davā 'medicine', हवा havā 'wind', आशा āśā 'hope' are feminine.

rules.title: Nouns in -ī are usually feminine
rules.body: Most nouns ending in -ī (-ई) are feminine: लड़की laṛkī 'girl', कुर्सी kursī 'chair', रोटी roṭī 'bread', नदी nadī 'river', गाड़ी gāṛī 'car, vehicle'. Important masculine exceptions: पानी pānī 'water', आदमी ādmī 'man', हाथी hāthī 'elephant', दही dahī 'yoghurt', घी ghī 'ghee', मोती motī 'pearl', and the respectful word जी jī.

rules.title: Other endings: learn the gender, use the hints
rules.body: Nouns ending in a consonant or other vowel can be either gender: घर ghar, दिन din, फल phal, मकान makān are m.; किताब kitāb, मेज़ mez, रात rāt, बात bāt, सड़क saṛak are f. Helpful tendencies: abstract nouns in -ता -tā, -आई -āī and -अट -aṭ are feminine (सुंदरता sundartā 'beauty', पढ़ाई paṛhāī 'studies', सजावट sajāvaṭ 'decoration'); nouns in -पन -pan and -आव -āv are masculine (बचपन bachpan 'childhood', बदलाव badlāv 'change').

rules.title: Plural of masculine nouns
rules.body: Masculine nouns in -ā change -ā to -e in the plural: लड़का → लड़के laṛke, कमरा → कमरे kamre, बेटा → बेटे beṭe. All other masculine nouns are unchanged in the direct plural: घर → घर, आदमी → आदमी, फल → फल; a number or word like कई kaī 'several' makes the plural clear: दो घर 'two houses'. A few masculine -ā nouns for people, mostly relationship terms and Sanskrit words, also stay unchanged: पिता pitā 'father', राजा rājā 'king', नेता netā 'leader', चाचा chāchā 'uncle'.

rules.title: Plural of feminine nouns in -ī
rules.body: Feminine nouns in -ī form the plural with -iyān: the ī shortens to i and -याँ is added: लड़की → लड़कियाँ laṛkiyān, कुर्सी → कुर्सियाँ kursiyān, रोटी → रोटियाँ roṭiyān, नदी → नदियाँ nadiyān. Feminine nouns already ending in -iyā just add the nasal: चिड़िया chiṛiyā 'bird' → चिड़ियाँ chiṛiyān, गुड़िया guṛiyā 'doll' → गुड़ियाँ.

rules.title: Plural of other feminine nouns
rules.body: Feminine nouns not ending in -ī add -ें -en: किताब → किताबें kitāben, मेज़ → मेज़ें mezen, रात → रातें rāten, बात → बातें bāten. After a vowel the ending is written -एँ: भाषा → भाषाएँ bhāṣāen, माता → माताएँ mātāen, वस्तु vastu 'thing' → वस्तुएँ; a long ū shortens: बहू bahū 'daughter-in-law' → बहुएँ bahuen.

rules.title: Making feminine forms of people and animals
rules.body: Nouns for people and animals often come in pairs. Masculine -ā becomes feminine -ī: लड़का/लड़की, बेटा/बेटी beṭā/beṭī, घोड़ा/घोड़ी ghoṛā/ghoṛī 'horse/mare', चाचा/चाची. Other words add -नी -nī: शेर/शेरनी śer/śernī 'lion/lioness', मोर/मोरनी 'peacock/peahen', ऊँट/ऊँटनी 'camel'. Some use -इन -in: मालिक/मालकिन mālik/mālkin 'master/mistress', धोबी/धोबिन 'washerman/washerwoman'. Professions such as डॉक्टर ḍŏkṭar and अध्यापक adhyāpak are often used for both sexes, with the verb showing gender.

rules.title: Plural for respect
rules.body: A single respected person is referred to with plural forms: पिता जी आए हैं pitā jī āe hain 'father has come' (lit. 'have come'). The honorific जी after a name or kinship term goes with this plural: दादी जी घर पर हैं 'grandma is at home'. Some nouns are used only in the plural: लोग log 'people' (दो लोग 'two people'). After a number the noun takes the plural, unlike in some languages: पाँच किताबें, तीन लड़के.

rules.title: Gender of loanwords
rules.body: English and other loanwords also get a gender, usually by analogy with a Hindi word of similar meaning or by sound. Feminine: कार kār, बस bas, ट्रेन ṭren, गाड़ी gāṛī, चाय chāy 'tea', कॉफ़ी kŏfī, फ़िल्म film, टीम ṭīm. Masculine: फ़ोन fon, कंप्यूटर kampyūṭar, स्कूल skūl, स्टेशन sṭeśan, होटल hoṭal. Most of these do not change in the direct plural unless feminine: बसें basen 'buses', फ़िल्में filmen 'films'.

exercises.q: The gender of लड़की (girl) is
exercises.explain: लड़की refers to a female and ends in -ī: feminine.

exercises.q: कमरा (room) is
options: feminine, because it is a loanword
exercises.explain: Nouns in -ā are mostly masculine: कमरा, केला, बेटा.

exercises.q: Most nouns ending in -ī are feminine.
exercises.explain: लड़की, कुर्सी, रोटी, नदी are feminine; पानी and आदमी are exceptions.

exercises.q: Plural of लड़का (boy): ___
exercises.explain: Masculine -ā nouns change -ā to -e in the plural.

exercises.q: Plural of लड़की (girl): ___
exercises.explain: Feminine -ī nouns shorten the ī and add -याँ.

exercises.q: Which noun is masculine despite ending in -ī?
exercises.explain: पानी 'water' is masculine: पानी ठंडा है; the others are regular feminines.

exercises.q: घर (house) changes in the direct plural: घर → घरे.
exercises.explain: Masculine nouns not ending in -ā are unchanged: दो घर 'two houses'.

exercises.q: The plural of किताब (book) is
exercises.explain: Feminine nouns not in -ī add -ें; किताबों is the oblique plural used only before postpositions.

exercises.q: Plural of कमरा (room): ___
exercises.explain: Masculine -ā → -e: कमरा → कमरे.

exercises.q: माता (mother) and भाषा (language) are feminine even though they end in -ā.
exercises.explain: These Sanskrit-origin words are exceptions to the -ā = masculine pattern.

exercises.q: Which noun is feminine?
exercises.explain: मेज़ 'table' is feminine (मेज़ बड़ी है); घर, फल and कमरा are masculine.

exercises.q: Plural of भाषा (language): ___
exercises.explain: Feminine nouns ending in a vowel other than -ī add -एँ.

exercises.q: The feminine of घोड़ा (horse) is
exercises.explain: Masculine -ā pairs with feminine -ī: घोड़ा / घोड़ी.

exercises.q: आदमी (man) is masculine and its direct plural is unchanged: दो आदमी.
exercises.explain: आदमी is a masculine -ī exception, and masculine nouns not in -ā do not change in the plural.

exercises.q: Plural of रात (night): ___
exercises.explain: रात is feminine and ends in a consonant, so it adds -ें.

exercises.q: Which plural is correct?
exercises.explain: रोटी is feminine in -ī: the ī shortens to i and -याँ is added.

exercises.q: Abstract nouns ending in -ता, such as सुंदरता (beauty), are usually feminine.
exercises.explain: -ता and -आई abstract nouns are feminine: सुंदरता, पढ़ाई, लड़ाई.

exercises.answer: मेरी बहनें दिल्ली में रहती हैं।

exercises.q: Plural of चिड़िया (bird): ___
exercises.explain: Feminine nouns in -iyā just add the nasal: चिड़िया → चिड़ियाँ.

exercises.q: Which pair shows a masculine -ā noun with its correct plural?
exercises.explain: बेटा is masculine, so -ā becomes -e; बेटियाँ is the plural of feminine बेटी.

exercises.q: In पिता जी आए हैं, the plural verb is used for one respected person.
exercises.explain: Hindi uses plural forms to show respect, especially with जी.

exercises.q: The loanword चाय (tea) is
exercises.explain: चाय is feminine, so the adjective takes -ī: चाय अच्छी है.

sections.title: Pronouns and the three levels of 'you'
sections.summary: Hindi has three words for 'you' (तू, तुम, आप) chosen by closeness and respect, and its pronouns change shape before postpositions. This chapter covers the personal pronouns, यह/वह, the oblique and contracted forms like मुझे and तुम्हें, and matching imperatives.

rules.title: The personal pronouns
rules.body: Subject pronouns: मैं main 'I', हम ham 'we', तू tū / तुम tum / आप āp 'you', यह yah 'this, he, she, it (near)', वह vah 'that, he, she, it (far)', ये ye 'these, they (near)', वे ve 'those, they (far)'. In speech यह and वह are pronounced ye and vo, and ये/वे both sound like ye/vo too; the spelling stays यह/वह/ये/वे in writing.

rules.title: Three levels of 'you': तू, तुम, आप
rules.body: तू tū is intimate: for God, small children, very close friends in some families, and also as an insult to strangers; it takes singular verb forms (तू है). तुम tum is familiar: friends, younger people, equals; it takes its own form हो (तुम हो). आप āp is respectful: elders, strangers, teachers, customers; it takes plural forms (आप हैं). When in doubt use आप. Many families use आप even for children, and तू is best avoided by learners.

rules.title: तुम and आप are grammatically plural
rules.body: तुम and आप take the same verb forms whether you address one person or several. To make clear that you mean more than one person, add लोग log 'people': तुम लोग tum log, आप लोग āp log; the same works for हम लोग 'we (all)'. Likewise one respected person is referred to with plural ये/वे and plural verbs.

examples.target: हम लोग दिल्ली में रहते हैं।
examples.roman: ham log dillī men rahte hain.

rules.title: यह / वह and ये / वे: no gender, but number and respect
rules.body: यह (near) and वह (far) mean this/that and also he/she/it; the pronoun itself has no gender, so the verb or adjective shows it: वह आता है 'he comes', वह आती है 'she comes'. The plurals ये/वे mean these/those/they and are also used for one respected person: ये मेरे पिता हैं ye mere pitā hain 'this is my father'. वह/वे are the default for 'he/she/they' when the person is not present.

rules.title: Oblique pronouns before postpositions
rules.body: Before a postposition (से, को, में, पर, का...) several pronouns change: मैं → मुझ mujh, तू → तुझ tujh, यह → इस is, वह → उस us, ये → इन in, वे → उन un, कौन/क्या → किस kis (pl. किन kin). हम, तुम and आप do not change. Simple postpositions are often written joined to the pronoun: मुझसे, उसको, इनमें.

rules.title: Contracted forms with को: मुझे, तुम्हें, उसे...
rules.body: Pronoun + को has a short, very common form: मुझे mujhe (= मुझको), तुझे tujhe, तुम्हें tumhen, हमें hamen, इसे ise, उसे use, इन्हें inhen, उन्हें unhen, किसे kise 'to whom'. आप has no contraction: आपको āpko. These forms are used for indirect objects, direct objects and in 'experiencer' patterns such as liking and needing.

examples.en: I need tea. (lit. to me tea is needed)

rules.title: Possessive pronouns
rules.body: The possessives are मेरा merā 'my', हमारा hamārā 'our', तेरा terā 'your (तू)', तुम्हारा tumhārā 'your (तुम)', आपका āpkā 'your (आप)', इसका iskā / उसका uskā 'his, her, its', इनका inkā / उनका unkā 'their', किसका kiskā 'whose'. They behave like -ā adjectives and agree with the thing owned: मेरा भाई, मेरी बहन, मेरे भाई (chapter 6 has the details).

rules.title: अपना 'one's own' and ख़ुद 'oneself'
rules.body: When the owner is the subject of the sentence, use अपना apnā (-ā/-ī/-e) instead of मेरा, उसका etc.: मैं अपनी किताब पढ़ता हूँ 'I read my (own) book', वह अपना काम करता है 'he does his (own) work'. Using उसका here would mean someone else's. ख़ुद khud or स्वयं svayam means 'oneself, personally': मैं ख़ुद जाऊँगा 'I will go myself'.

rules.title: Question and indefinite pronouns
rules.body: कौन kaun 'who', क्या kyā 'what', कोई koī 'someone, any(one)', कुछ kuchh 'something, some', सब sab 'all, everyone'. Before postpositions: कौन/क्या → किस kis (किसको / किसे 'to whom', किसका 'whose'), कोई → किसी kisī (किसी को 'to someone'); कुछ and सब do not change.

examples.target: आप किससे बात कर रहे हैं?
examples.roman: āp kisse bāt kar rahe hain?

rules.title: Imperatives match the level of 'you'
rules.body: Commands change with the pronoun: तू takes the bare stem (जा jā 'go', बैठ baiṭh 'sit'); तुम takes -ओ (जाओ jāo, बैठो baiṭho); आप takes -इए (जाइए jāie, बैठिए baiṭhie). Irregular with आप: करना → कीजिए kījie, देना → दीजिए dījie, लेना → लीजिए lījie, पीना → पीजिए pījie. An even softer request adds -गा: आइएगा āiegā 'please do come'.

exercises.q: Which 'you' is used for an elder or a stranger?
exercises.explain: आप is the respectful 'you'; तुम is familiar, तू intimate, वह means he/she.

exercises.q: मैं means
exercises.explain: मैं main is 'I'; हम is 'we'.

exercises.q: तुम takes the verb form हो: तुम कहाँ हो?
exercises.explain: हो is the special form of 'to be' used only with तुम.

exercises.q: ___ कहाँ हैं? (you, polite)
exercises.explain: The respectful आप takes the plural verb हैं.

exercises.q: Which sentence is correct with तू?
exercises.explain: तू takes the singular form है, like वह.

exercises.q: वह can mean he, she or it; the pronoun itself shows no gender.
exercises.explain: Gender is shown by the verb or adjective: वह आता है / वह आती है.

exercises.q: मैं changes before a postposition: ___ से (from me)
exercises.explain: The oblique of मैं is मुझ: मुझसे, मुझको, मुझमें.

exercises.q: The contracted form of मुझ को is
exercises.explain: मुझे = मुझको 'to me'; मैंने is the ergative form and मेरा is 'my'.

exercises.q: ___ चाय चाहिए। (to me, contracted form: 'I need tea')
exercises.explain: Needs are expressed with the को-form of the person: मुझे ... चाहिए.

exercises.q: आप को has a contracted form आपे.
exercises.explain: आप has no contraction; you say आपको.

exercises.q: To make clear that you are addressing several people politely, you say
exercises.explain: लोग 'people' is added because आप alone can be singular or plural.

exercises.q: वह changes before a postposition: ___ को (to him / her)
exercises.explain: The oblique of वह is उस; उसको contracts to उसे.

exercises.q: ये मेरे पिता हैं uses plural ये and हैं because
options: plural forms show respect for an elder
the verb is in the past
exercises.explain: One respected person is referred to with plural pronoun and verb.

exercises.q: तू is a safe, neutral form to use with shopkeepers and strangers.
exercises.explain: तू to a stranger sounds rude or insulting; use आप.

exercises.q: Contracted form of उन को (to them): ___
exercises.explain: उन + को contracts to उन्हें, just as इन को becomes इन्हें.

exercises.q: मैं ___ किताब पढ़ता हूँ। (I read my own book)
exercises.explain: The owner is the subject, so अपना is used, and it takes -ī to agree with किताब (f.).

exercises.q: In speech, यह and वह are commonly pronounced ye and vo.
exercises.explain: The written forms यह/वह keep the h, but everyday pronunciation is ye and vo.

exercises.q: ___ को बुलाओ। (someone: oblique of कोई)
exercises.explain: कोई becomes किसी before a postposition.

exercises.q: Which command is NOT standard?
exercises.explain: आप takes the -इए imperative; -ओ belongs to तुम.

exercises.en: We (all) will go to Delhi tomorrow.

exercises.q: Which pronoun does NOT change before a postposition?
exercises.explain: हम, तुम and आप stay the same; मैं → मुझ, वह → उस, यह → इस.

exercises.q: हमें is the contracted form of हम को.
exercises.explain: हम + को → हमें 'to us', parallel to तुम्हें.

sections.title: 'To be' and the present tense
sections.summary: The verb होना 'to be' (हूँ, है, हैं, हो) is the backbone of Hindi sentences and the auxiliary of the habitual present. Here you learn its forms, the verb-final word order, and how to build 'I speak / she goes' with -ता/-ती/-ते plus होना.

rules.title: Present tense of होना 'to be'
rules.body: मैं हूँ main hūn 'I am'; तू है tū hai; यह/वह है yah/vah hai 'he, she, it is'; हम हैं ham hain 'we are'; तुम हो tum ho; आप हैं āp hain; ये/वे हैं ye/ve hain 'they are'. Note that है (singular) and हैं (plural, with the nasal dot) look alike but are different forms, and that हो is only used with तुम.

rules.title: Word order: the verb comes last
rules.body: Hindi is subject-object-verb. The verb (with its auxiliary) sits at the end: मैं हिंदी बोलता हूँ 'I Hindi speak am'. Time words come early, place before the verb, and question words usually sit just before the verb rather than at the start: आप कहाँ रहते हैं? 'Where do you live?'

examples.en: I go to school every day.

rules.title: The habitual present: stem + -ता/-ती/-ते + होना
rules.body: Take the infinitive, drop -ना to get the stem (बोलना → बोल), add -ता (m. sg.), -ते (m. pl.) or -ती (f.), then the matching form of होना: मैं बोलता हूँ (man) / मैं बोलती हूँ (woman) 'I speak', वह जाता है 'he goes', हम खाते हैं 'we eat', वे पढ़ते हैं 'they read'. Stems ending in a vowel just take the ending: जा-ता, खा-ती, पी-ते, सो-ता.

rules.title: Agreement is by gender and number, not person
rules.body: The -ता/-ती/-ते ending agrees with the subject's gender and number, while होना adds the person: लड़का जाता है, लड़के जाते हैं, लड़की जाती है, लड़कियाँ जाती हैं. तुम takes -ते हो (men) or -ती हो (women); आप takes -ते हैं or -ती हैं. Feminine uses the same -ती for singular and plural; the auxiliary (है/हैं) shows the number.

examples.en: What do you do? (to a man)
What do you do? (to a woman)

rules.title: Common verbs and their stems
rules.body: Useful infinitives and stems: करना karnā → कर 'do', जाना → जा 'go', आना → आ 'come', खाना → खा 'eat', पीना → पी 'drink', देखना → देख 'see', सुनना → सुन 'hear', बोलना → बोल 'speak', पढ़ना paṛhnā → पढ़ 'read, study', लिखना → लिख 'write', रहना → रह 'live, stay', सोना → सो 'sleep', समझना → समझ 'understand', चाहना → चाह 'want'.

rules.title: What the habitual present is used for
rules.body: The -ता हूँ form expresses habits and repeated actions (मैं रोज़ दौड़ता हूँ 'I run every day'), general truths (सूरज पूर्व में निकलता है 'the sun rises in the east'), and states with verbs like जानना 'know', समझना, चाहना, रहना. For an action happening right now Hindi uses the continuous (chapter 8), not this form.

examples.en: The sun rises in the east.

rules.title: Negation: नहीं before the verb
rules.body: नहीं nahīn goes right before the verb: मैं हिंदी नहीं बोलता 'I don't speak Hindi'. In the negative habitual the auxiliary हूँ/है/हैं is usually dropped. When it is dropped, a feminine plural verb takes a nasal ending: वे नहीं जातीं ve nahīn jātīn 'they (f.) don't go'. With plain होना the auxiliary stays: वह यहाँ नहीं है 'he is not here'.

rules.title: 'There is': existence and location with होना
rules.body: होना also states that something exists or where it is; there is no separate word for 'there is': कमरे में एक मेज़ है 'there is a table in the room', दिल्ली में बहुत लोग हैं 'there are many people in Delhi'. The place phrase (with में 'in' or पर 'on, at') comes before the verb.

examples.en: There is a table in the room.
There are books on the table.

rules.title: है versus होता है
rules.body: Plain है describes the situation now; the habitual होता है describes what is generally or usually the case. यहाँ गर्मी है 'it is hot here (now)' versus यहाँ गर्मी होती है 'it is (usually) hot here'. यह मुश्किल है 'this is difficult' versus यह मुश्किल होता है 'this (kind of thing) is difficult'.

exercises.explain: हूँ is the first person singular of होना.

exercises.q: तुम ___ (you are, familiar)
exercises.explain: हो is used only with तुम.

exercises.q: आप takes हैं even when speaking to one person.
exercises.explain: आप is grammatically plural, so it always takes हैं.

exercises.q: वे छात्र ___। (they are students)
exercises.explain: Plural वे takes हैं with the nasal dot.

exercises.q: The stem of बोलना (to speak) is
exercises.explain: Drop -ना from the infinitive to get the stem.

exercises.q: मैं हिंदी ___ हूँ। (speak; a man speaking)
exercises.explain: Masculine singular habitual: stem + -ता.

exercises.q: A woman saying 'I eat' says मैं खाती हूँ.
exercises.explain: Feminine subjects take -ती; the person is shown by हूँ.

exercises.q: लड़कियाँ स्कूल ___ हैं।
exercises.explain: Feminine plural uses -ती plus हैं.

exercises.q: हम रोज़ चाय ___ हैं। (drink; a group of men or mixed group)
exercises.explain: Masculine plural habitual: stem पी + -ते.

exercises.q: The Hindi verb normally comes at the end of the sentence.
exercises.explain: Hindi is subject-object-verb: मैं चाय पीता हूँ.

exercises.q: आप क्या ___ हैं? (what do you do? asking a man)
exercises.explain: आप takes the plural -ते form with हैं.

exercises.q: तुम कहाँ ___ हो? (live; to a man)
exercises.explain: तुम takes the plural-type -ते with हो.

exercises.q: Which negative sentence is in the standard order?
exercises.explain: नहीं goes right before the verb; the auxiliary is usually dropped.

exercises.q: In the negative habitual the auxiliary हूँ/है/हैं is often dropped: वह नहीं आता.
exercises.explain: वह नहीं आता is the normal way to say 'he doesn't come'.

exercises.q: कमरे में एक मेज़ ___। (there is)
exercises.explain: Existence is expressed with plain होना: 'in the room a table is'.

exercises.q: यहाँ गर्मी होती है means
options: It is hot here right now
exercises.explain: The habitual होता है states what is generally the case.

exercises.answer: मेरी बहन दिल्ली में काम करती है।

exercises.q: The habitual ending -ता/-ती/-ते agrees with the person (I, you, he), not with gender.
exercises.explain: It agrees with gender and number; the person is shown by हूँ/हो/है/हैं.

exercises.q: वे लड़कियाँ नहीं ___। (go; negative, auxiliary dropped)
exercises.explain: When the auxiliary is dropped, feminine plural takes the nasalised -तीं.

exercises.q: आप ___ हैं? (do you understand? asking a woman)
exercises.explain: A female addressee takes -ती; आप still takes हैं.

exercises.q: Which sentence states a general truth?
options: पानी सौ डिग्री पर उबलता है।
exercises.explain: The habitual -ता है is used for general truths; the others are continuous, past and future.

exercises.q: मैं समझता हूँ is a correct present form meaning 'I understand'.
exercises.explain: Verbs of knowing and understanding use the habitual, not the continuous.

sections.title: Postpositions and the oblique case
sections.summary: Hindi puts its 'prepositions' after the noun, and the noun or pronoun in front of them switches to the oblique case. This chapter covers में, पर, से, को, तक, का/की/के and the compound postpositions, and how nouns, adjectives and pronouns change before them.

rules.title: Postpositions follow the noun
rules.body: Where English says 'in the house', Hindi says घर में ghar men 'house in'. The basic postpositions are में men 'in', पर par 'on, at', से se 'from, with, by', को ko 'to', तक tak 'until, up to', and का/की/के kā/kī/ke 'of'. They are written as separate words after nouns, and usually joined to pronouns (मुझसे, उसको).

rules.title: The oblique singular
rules.body: A noun followed by a postposition is in the oblique case. Masculine nouns in -ā change -ā to -e: लड़का → लड़के को laṛke ko, कमरा → कमरे में kamre men, बेटा → बेटे से. All other singular nouns are unchanged: घर में, आदमी को, लड़की को, किताब में. So लड़के can be either 'boys' (direct plural) or 'boy' before a postposition.

rules.title: The oblique plural: always -ों
rules.body: Before a postposition every plural noun ends in -ों -on: लड़कों को laṛkon ko 'to the boys', घरों में gharon men 'in the houses', किताबों में kitābon men 'in the books', बातों से. Feminine -ī nouns use -ियों: लड़कियों से laṛkiyon se; nouns in -ū shorten it: आलुओं में āluon men. Honorific plurals do the same: पिता जी को... but बच्चों को 'to the children'.

rules.title: का / की / के: 'of' agrees with the thing owned
rules.body: Possession uses का after the owner, and it agrees like an adjective with the possessed noun: राम का घर rām kā ghar 'Ram's house' (m. sg.), राम की किताब 'Ram's book' (f.), राम के बच्चे 'Ram's children' (m. pl.). When the possessed noun is itself followed by a postposition, का becomes के: राम के घर में 'in Ram's house', राम के बेटे को 'to Ram's son'.

rules.title: को: to, for the object, and in time expressions
rules.body: को marks the indirect object (राम को दो 'give to Ram'), the direct object when it is a specific person or thing (मैं राम को जानता हूँ 'I know Ram'; किताब को उठाओ 'pick up the book'), and the experiencer in patterns like मुझे पसंद है, मुझे चाहिए. It is also used with days and times of day: सोमवार को 'on Monday', रात को 'at night', शाम को 'in the evening'.

rules.title: से: from, with (instrument), by, than
rules.body: से means 'from' (दिल्ली से 'from Delhi'), 'with' an instrument (चम्मच से 'with a spoon'), 'by' a means of transport (बस से 'by bus'), and 'than' in comparisons (राम से लंबा 'taller than Ram'). Several verbs take से where English uses 'to': पूछना 'ask', बात करना 'talk', मिलना 'meet', कहना 'say', डरना 'fear'. For 'together with' a person use के साथ.

examples.target: वह बस से स्कूल जाता है।
examples.roman: vah bas se skūl jātā hai.
examples.en: He goes to school by bus.

examples.target: मैं राम से बात करता हूँ।
examples.roman: main rām se bāt kartā hūn.

rules.title: में versus पर
rules.body: में is 'in, inside': दिल्ली में, घर में, पानी में. पर is 'on' a surface and 'at' a point or place: मेज़ पर 'on the table', स्टेशन पर 'at the station', दरवाज़े पर 'at the door', घर पर 'at home'. Note घर में 'inside the house' versus घर पर 'at home'. Cities and countries take में.

rules.title: Compound postpositions with के / की
rules.body: Many postpositions are two words beginning with के: के पास ke pās 'near; in the possession of', के लिए ke lie 'for', के साथ ke sāth 'with', के बाद ke bād 'after', से पहले se pahle 'before', के सामने ke sāmne 'in front of', के पीछे ke pīchhe 'behind', के अंदर 'inside', के बाहर 'outside', के बारे में ke bāre men 'about'. A few take की: की तरफ़ kī taraf 'towards', की तरह kī tarah 'like', की वजह से kī vajah se 'because of'. Pronouns take their possessive form before them: मेरे लिए, आपके साथ, उसकी तरफ़.

rules.title: Adjectives and demonstratives go oblique too
rules.body: Everything in front of the noun agrees with the oblique: -ā adjectives take -e, and यह/वह become इस/उस, ये/वे become इन/उन: बड़ा कमरा → बड़े कमरे में 'in the big room', यह घर → इस घर में 'in this house', वे लड़के → उन लड़कों को 'to those boys'. Feminine adjectives do not change: छोटी लड़की को. Possessives also take -e: मेरा बेटा → मेरे बेटे को.

rules.title: तक, के पास and 'to have'
rules.body: तक is 'until, up to, as far as': दो बजे तक 'until two o'clock', स्टेशन तक 'as far as the station'. के पास means 'near' (घर के पास 'near the house') and is the usual way to say 'have' for things you can carry or own: मेरे पास गाड़ी है 'I have a car', आपके पास पैसे हैं? 'do you have money?'. Chapter 6 compares this with का and को possession.

exercises.q: The postposition meaning 'in' is
exercises.explain: में men = in; पर = on/at, से = from, को = to.

exercises.q: Hindi postpositions
exercises.explain: घर में 'in the house' literally says 'house in'.

exercises.q: मेज़ पर means 'on the table'.
exercises.explain: पर is 'on' a surface or 'at' a point.

exercises.q: लड़का before a postposition: ___ को (to the boy)
exercises.explain: Masculine -ā nouns take -e in the oblique singular.

exercises.q: कमरा + में =
exercises.explain: Oblique singular of कमरा is कमरे; कमरों is the oblique plural.

exercises.q: मैं दिल्ली ___ हूँ। (from)
exercises.explain: से marks origin: दिल्ली से 'from Delhi'.

exercises.en: The book is on the table.

exercises.q: Feminine singular nouns do not change before a postposition: लड़की को.
exercises.explain: Only masculine -ā nouns change in the oblique singular.

exercises.q: The oblique plural of घर (before a postposition) is
exercises.explain: All plural nouns take -ों before a postposition: घरों में.

exercises.q: लड़कियाँ before a postposition: ___ से (from the girls)
exercises.explain: Feminine -ī nouns take -ियों in the oblique plural.

exercises.q: का/की/के agrees with the owner, not with the thing owned.
exercises.explain: It agrees with the possessed noun: राम की किताब because किताब is feminine.

exercises.q: मैं राम ___ जानता हूँ। (I know Ram)
exercises.explain: A specific person as direct object takes को.

exercises.q: यह किताब ___ के लिए है। (for you, polite)
exercises.explain: आप does not change before postpositions: आपके लिए.

exercises.answer: वह बस से स्कूल जाता है।
exercises.en: He goes to school by bus.

exercises.q: Which compound postposition means 'near / in the possession of'?
exercises.explain: के पास is 'near' and is used for having things: मेरे पास किताब है.

exercises.q: बड़ा कमरा → ___ कमरे में (in the big room)
exercises.explain: -ā adjectives take -e before an oblique noun.

exercises.q: सोमवार को means 'on Monday'.
exercises.explain: को is used with days and times of day: रात को, शाम को.

exercises.q: मुझ___ पूछो। (ask me)
exercises.explain: पूछना takes से for the person asked: मुझसे पूछो.

exercises.q: वह ___ घर में रहता है। (this; oblique form)
exercises.explain: यह becomes इस before an oblique noun with a postposition.

exercises.answer: मेरे दोस्त के पास नई गाड़ी है।
exercises.en: My friend has a new car.

exercises.q: दिल्ली पर is the normal way to say 'in Delhi'.
exercises.explain: Cities take में: दिल्ली में.

exercises.q: Which phrase is correct for 'to those boys'?
exercises.explain: Both the demonstrative (वे → उन) and the noun (लड़कों) go oblique plural.

exercises.q: राम ___ बहन (Ram's sister)
exercises.explain: बहन is feminine, so 'of' takes the form की.

exercises.q: Before a compound postposition like के लिए, मैं becomes मेरे: मेरे लिए.
exercises.explain: Compound postpositions take the possessive form of pronouns: मेरे लिए, आपके साथ.

exercises.answer: हम शाम को बाज़ार जाते हैं।
exercises.en: We go to the market in the evening.

exercises.q: मैं चम्मच ___ खाता हूँ। (with a spoon)
exercises.explain: Instruments take से; के साथ is for company (people).

sections.title: Possession and adjectives
sections.summary: Possessives like मेरा/मेरी/मेरे and adjectives ending in -ā change with the gender, number and case of the noun they describe, while adjectives with other endings never change. This chapter also covers the three ways of saying 'have', अपना, and comparison with से and सबसे.

rules.title: मेरा / मेरी / मेरे agree with the thing owned
rules.body: Possessive pronouns agree with the possessed noun, not with the owner: मेरा बेटा merā beṭā 'my son' (m. sg.), मेरी बेटी merī beṭī 'my daughter' (f. sg. and pl.: मेरी बेटियाँ), मेरे बेटे mere beṭe 'my sons' (m. pl.). The -e form is also used before any masculine singular noun followed by a postposition: मेरे बेटे को 'to my son', मेरे घर में 'in my house'.

rules.title: The full set of possessives
rules.body: All possessives follow the same -ā/-ī/-e pattern: मेरा 'my', हमारा hamārā 'our', तेरा terā 'your (तू)', तुम्हारा tumhārā 'your (तुम)', आपका āpkā 'your (आप)', इसका iskā / उसका uskā 'his, her, its', इनका inkā / उनका unkā 'their (and his/her, respectful)', किसका kiskā 'whose', अपना apnā 'one's own'. Note the vowel change in हमारा and तुम्हारा.

rules.title: Adjectives in -ā agree with the noun
rules.body: Adjectives come before the noun. Those ending in -ā take -ā with a masculine singular noun, -e with a masculine plural or oblique noun, and -ī with any feminine noun: अच्छा लड़का achchhā laṛkā, अच्छे लड़के, अच्छी लड़की, अच्छी लड़कियाँ. Common -ā adjectives: बड़ा baṛā 'big', छोटा chhoṭā 'small', नया nayā 'new' (f. नई naī, m. pl. नए nae), पुराना purānā 'old', लंबा lambā 'tall', सस्ता sastā 'cheap', काला kālā 'black'.

rules.title: Invariable adjectives never change
rules.body: Adjectives that do not end in -ā keep one form everywhere: सुंदर sundar 'beautiful', लाल lāl 'red', साफ़ sāf 'clean', ठीक ṭhīk 'fine', गरम garam 'hot' (but ठंडा ṭhanḍā 'cold' ends in -ā and does change), ख़ुश khush 'happy', ख़राब kharāb 'bad', मुश्किल muśkil 'difficult', आसान āsān 'easy', ख़ूबसूरत khūbsūrat 'beautiful'. A few adjectives in -ā borrowed from Persian or Arabic are also invariable: ज़िंदा zindā 'alive', बढ़िया baṛhiyā 'excellent', उम्दा umdā 'fine', ताज़ा tāzā 'fresh' (though ताज़ी is heard).

rules.title: Adjectives after 'to be' also agree
rules.body: Predicate adjectives follow the same agreement: लड़की लंबी है 'the girl is tall', लड़के लंबे हैं 'the boys are tall', कमरे साफ़ हैं 'the rooms are clean' (invariable). With आप and other honorific plurals the adjective takes the plural form: आप अच्छे हैं (to a man), आप अच्छी हैं (to a woman). Adjectives can also stand alone as nouns: बड़े 'the elders', छोटे 'the little ones'.

examples.target: आप कैसे हैं? - मैं ठीक हूँ।
examples.roman: āp kaise hain? - main ṭhīk hūn.
examples.en: How are you? - I am fine.

rules.title: Three ways to say 'have'
rules.body: Hindi has no verb 'to have'. For things you can carry or own, use के पास: मेरे पास गाड़ी है 'I have a car'. For relatives, body parts and inalienable things, use का/की/के: मेरे दो भाई हैं 'I have two brothers', उसकी आँखें नीली हैं 'she has blue eyes'. For feelings, illnesses and needs, use the को form: मुझे बुख़ार है 'I have a fever', मुझे ज़ुकाम है 'I have a cold'.

rules.title: अपना: when the owner is the subject
rules.body: अपना apnā (-ā/-ī/-e) replaces मेरा, तुम्हारा, उसका and so on when the owner is the subject of the clause: वह अपनी माँ से मिलता है 'he meets his (own) mother'; वह उसकी माँ से मिलता है would mean someone else's mother. मैं अपना काम करता हूँ 'I do my work'; तुम अपनी किताब लाओ 'bring your book'. In the main 'to be' sentence the ordinary possessive is used: यह मेरी किताब है.

examples.target: वह अपनी माँ से मिलता है।
examples.roman: vah apnī mān se miltā hai.

examples.target: वह उसकी माँ से मिलता है।
examples.roman: vah uskī mān se miltā hai.

rules.title: Comparison with से and सबसे
rules.body: There are no comparative endings. 'X is taller than Y' is X Y से लंबा है: राम श्याम से लंबा है. To stress use ज़्यादा zyādā 'more' or कम kam 'less': यह उससे ज़्यादा सस्ता है 'this is cheaper than that'. The superlative uses सबसे sabse 'than all': सबसे बड़ा 'the biggest', सबसे अच्छी फ़िल्म 'the best film'. बहुत bahut 'very' and थोड़ा thoṛā 'a little' modify adjectives.

rules.title: Demonstratives and 'which' as adjectives
rules.body: यह/वह and ये/वे also work as adjectives: यह किताब 'this book', वह लड़का 'that boy', ये किताबें 'these books'; before a postposition they become इस/उस/इन/उन: इस किताब में. कौन सा kaun sā 'which' agrees like an -ā adjective: कौन सा लड़का, कौन सी किताब, कौन से लोग. ऐसा aisā 'such, like this' and वैसा vaisā 'like that' agree the same way.

exercises.q: ___ बेटी (my daughter)
exercises.explain: बेटी is feminine, so the possessive takes -ī.

exercises.q: अच्छा लड़का in the plural is
exercises.explain: Both the -ā adjective and the -ā noun take -e in the masculine plural.

exercises.q: Adjectives ending in -ā change to -ī before a feminine noun.
exercises.explain: बड़ा घर but बड़ी किताब.

exercises.q: यह ___ किताब है। (your, polite)
exercises.explain: किताब is feminine, so आपका becomes आपकी.

exercises.q: सुंदर (beautiful) before a feminine noun is
exercises.explain: Adjectives not ending in -ā are invariable.

exercises.q: ___ कमरा बड़ा है। (his / her, the person is not near)
exercises.explain: वह + का gives उसका, agreeing with masculine कमरा.

exercises.en: My mother is very good. (respectful plural verb)

exercises.q: लाल (red) becomes लाली before a feminine noun.
exercises.explain: लाल does not end in -ā, so it never changes: लाल किताब.

exercises.q: मेरे पास गाड़ी है means
exercises.explain: के पास is the usual way to say 'have' for possessions.

exercises.q: वह ___ काम करता है। (his own; m. sg. noun)
exercises.explain: The owner is the subject, so अपना is used; काम is masculine.

exercises.q: मुझे बुख़ार है (I have a fever) uses the को-form, not के पास.
exercises.explain: Illnesses and feelings are 'had' with को: मुझे बुख़ार है.

exercises.q: 'taller than Ram' is
exercises.explain: Comparison uses से 'than' after the thing compared.

exercises.q: यह ___ अच्छी फ़िल्म है। (the best: 'than all')
exercises.explain: सबसे + adjective makes the superlative.

exercises.q: Which adjective is invariable?
exercises.explain: ख़ुश does not end in -ā, so it has one form: वह ख़ुश है, वे ख़ुश हैं.

exercises.q: अच्छे ___ को (to the good boy; oblique singular)
exercises.explain: Before को, both the adjective and the masculine -ā noun take -e.

exercises.q: वह अपनी माँ से मिलता है means he meets his own mother.
exercises.explain: अपना refers back to the subject; उसकी माँ would be someone else's mother.

exercises.q: आप ___ हैं? (how are you? asking a woman)
exercises.explain: कैसा agrees with the person: feminine कैसी.

exercises.q: लड़कियाँ ___ हैं। (tall)
exercises.explain: Feminine adjectives take -ī for singular and plural alike.

exercises.answer: उसका भाई मेरे दोस्त से छोटा है।
exercises.en: His brother is younger than my friend.

exercises.q: In वह उसकी किताब पढ़ता है, the book belongs to someone other than the reader.
exercises.explain: For the reader's own book Hindi would say अपनी किताब.

exercises.q: ___ किताब आपकी है? (which book)
exercises.explain: कौन सा agrees with किताब (f.): कौन सी.

exercises.q: नया (new) in the feminine: ___
exercises.explain: नया → नई (f.), नए (m. pl.).

exercises.q: मेरे पास दो भाई हैं is the normal way to say 'I have two brothers'.
exercises.explain: Relatives are 'had' with का/के: मेरे दो भाई हैं.

exercises.answer: यह शहर दिल्ली से ज़्यादा सुंदर है।
exercises.en: This city is more beautiful than Delhi.

sections.title: Past and future
sections.summary: The past of 'to be' (था/थी/थे/थीं), the simple past of verbs (-ā/-ī/-e), the past habitual (-ता था) and the future (-ूँगा/-एगा/-एँगे) all agree with the subject's gender and number. This chapter shows the forms, the irregular verbs and the time words that go with them.

rules.title: The past of होना: था, थी, थे, थीं
rules.body: 'Was/were' agrees in gender and number: था thā (m. sg.), थी thī (f. sg.), थे the (m. pl., and with तुम/आप for men), थीं thīn (f. pl.). मैं घर पर था 'I (m.) was at home', वह ख़ुश थी 'she was happy', हम वहाँ थे 'we were there', लड़कियाँ स्कूल में थीं 'the girls were at school'.

rules.title: Simple past of intransitive verbs
rules.body: The simple past (perfective) is stem + -ā (m. sg.), -ī (f. sg.), -e (m. pl.), -īn (f. pl.): वह आया vah āyā 'he came', वह आई āī 'she came', वे आए āe 'they came', वे आईं āīn 'they (f.) came'. After a vowel stem a य is written before -ā: आया, सोया soyā, खाया. मैं गया / मैं गई 'I went' (m./f.). Transitive verbs behave the same but their subject takes ने (chapter 8).

rules.title: Irregular past forms
rules.body: Five common verbs have irregular past stems: जाना → गया/गई/गए/गईं gayā; होना → हुआ/हुई/हुए/हुईं huā 'happened, became'; करना → किया/की/किए/कीं kiyā; देना → दिया/दी/दिए/दीं diyā; लेना → लिया/ली/लिए/लीं liyā. पीना 'drink' gives पिया/पी/पिए/पीं. Note the feminine singular of करना, देना, लेना is simply की, दी, ली.

rules.title: Past habitual: -ता था 'used to'
rules.body: Habits and repeated actions in the past use the -ता/-ती/-ते form with था/थी/थे/थीं instead of the present auxiliary: मैं रोज़ स्कूल जाता था 'I used to go to school every day', वह चाय पीती थी 'she used to drink tea', हम साथ खेलते थे 'we used to play together'. It is also used for 'was (doing) regularly' in stories and descriptions.

examples.en: I used to go to school every day.

rules.title: Present perfect and past perfect
rules.body: Adding है/हैं to the simple past makes the present perfect ('has/have done'): वह बाज़ार गया है 'he has gone to the market', वे आए हैं 'they have come'. Adding था/थी/थे/थीं makes the past perfect ('had done'): वह गया था 'he had gone', लड़कियाँ आई थीं 'the girls had come'. When an auxiliary follows, the feminine plural loses its nasal: आईं → आई थीं.

examples.en: He has gone to the market.

rules.title: The future: -ूँगा, -एगा, -एँगे, -ओगे
rules.body: The future is the stem plus a person ending plus -गा/-गी/-गे: मैं जाऊँगा jāūngā (m.) / जाऊँगी jāūngī (f.); तू/वह/यह जाएगा jāegā / जाएगी; हम/वे/आप जाएँगे jāenge / जाएँगी; तुम जाओगे jāoge / जाओगी. The -गा part agrees in gender and number; the vowel before it shows the person. Consonant stems work the same: करूँगा, करेगा, करेंगे, करोगे.

rules.title: Future of होना and the presumptive 'must be'
rules.body: होना follows the regular pattern: हूँगा hūngā, होगा hogā, होंगे honge, होगे hoge (तुम), feminine हूँगी, होगी, होंगी. Besides 'will be', होगा often expresses a guess about the present: वह घर पर होगा 'he must be at home / he is probably at home', आप थके होंगे 'you must be tired'.

examples.en: The weather will be good tomorrow.

rules.title: Future spelling with vowel stems; लेना and देना
rules.body: Stems ending in a vowel add the endings directly: आना → आऊँगा, आएगा, आएँगे, आओगे; पीना → पिऊँगा, पिएगा, पिएँगे, पिओगे (the ī shortens); सोना → सोऊँगा, सोएगा. लेना and देना are irregular: लूँगा lūngā, लेगा legā, लेंगे lenge, लोगे loge; दूँगा dūngā, देगा degā, देंगे denge, दोगे doge.

examples.en: I will give you a call. (m.)

rules.title: Time words: कल, परसों, पहले
rules.body: कल kal means both 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow'; the verb tense tells which: वह कल आया 'he came yesterday', वह कल आएगा 'he will come tomorrow'. Likewise परसों parson is 'the day before yesterday' or 'the day after tomorrow'. Other useful words: आज āj 'today', अभी abhī 'right now', पहले pahle 'before, earlier', बाद में bād men 'later', अगले साल agle sāl 'next year', पिछले हफ़्ते pichhle hafte 'last week'.

examples.en: They will go to India next year.

exercises.q: मैं घर पर ___। (I was; a man speaking)
exercises.explain: था is masculine singular 'was'.

exercises.q: वह ख़ुश ___। (she was happy)
exercises.explain: थी is feminine singular.

exercises.q: हम takes थे in the past: हम वहाँ थे.
exercises.explain: थे is the masculine plural form, used with हम, आप, तुम and वे.

exercises.q: वह कल ___। (came; he)
exercises.explain: Simple past of आना, masculine singular: आया.

exercises.q: The simple past of जाना for a woman ('she went') is
exercises.explain: जाना has the irregular past stem ग-: गया, गई, गए, गईं.

exercises.q: लड़कियाँ बाज़ार ___। (went; feminine plural, no auxiliary)
exercises.explain: Feminine plural past takes -ईं when no auxiliary follows.

exercises.q: कल can mean both yesterday and tomorrow; the verb tense tells which.
exercises.explain: वह कल आया 'he came yesterday' vs वह कल आएगा 'he will come tomorrow'.

exercises.q: मैं रोज़ स्कूल ___ था। (I used to go)
exercises.explain: The past habitual is -ता + था.

exercises.q: वह चाय ___ थी। (used to drink; she)
exercises.explain: Feminine habitual पीती with past auxiliary थी.

exercises.q: The future ending -गी is used for feminine subjects: वह जाएगी.
exercises.explain: -गा/-गी/-गे agree in gender and number like adjectives.

exercises.q: हम कल ___। (we will come)
exercises.explain: हम takes -एँगे: आएँगे.

exercises.q: मैं कल फ़ोन ___। (will do; a man speaking)
exercises.explain: First person future: stem + -ूँगा.

exercises.en: They will go to India next year.

exercises.q: The future of देना with मैं (m.) is
exercises.explain: देना and लेना are irregular: दूँगा, लूँगा.

exercises.q: वह घर पर होगा can mean 'he must be at home' (a guess about now).
exercises.explain: The future of होना is often presumptive.

exercises.q: तुम कब ___? (will come; to a man)
exercises.explain: तुम takes -ओगे in the future.

exercises.q: वह बाज़ार गया है means
options: He has gone to the market
He went to the market yesterday
He will go to the market
He used to go to the market
exercises.explain: Past participle + है is the present perfect.

exercises.q: हम बच्चे ___। (were; a group of boys)
exercises.explain: Masculine plural past of होना is थे.

exercises.answer: मेरी बहन पहले मुंबई में रहती थी।
exercises.en: My sister used to live in Mumbai before.

exercises.q: The simple past of होना is हुआ / हुई / हुए / हुईं.
exercises.explain: क्या हुआ? 'What happened?'

exercises.q: Which is correct for 'the girls had come'?
exercises.explain: With an auxiliary the participle loses its nasal; only थीं carries it.

exercises.q: आप कहाँ ___? (will be; asking a man)
exercises.explain: आप takes the plural future होंगे.

exercises.q: The future of लेना with हम is लेएँगे.
exercises.explain: लेना is irregular: हम लेंगे.

exercises.en: The weather will be good tomorrow.

sections.title: The continuous and 'ne'
sections.summary: 'I am eating' is built with रहा/रही/रहे plus होना, and in perfective tenses the subject of a transitive verb takes the ergative marker ने while the verb agrees with the object. This chapter covers both patterns and the verbs that break the ने rule.

rules.title: The present continuous: stem + रहा + होना
rules.body: An action in progress uses the stem followed by रहा rahā (m. sg.), रही rahī (f.), रहे rahe (m. pl.) and the present of होना: मैं खा रहा हूँ 'I am eating' (m.), वह जा रही है 'she is going', वे पढ़ रहे हैं 'they are reading'. रहा is a separate word and agrees with the subject; the stem never changes.

examples.en: She is going to the market.

rules.title: The past continuous: रहा था
rules.body: Replace the present auxiliary with था/थी/थे/थीं: मैं खा रहा था 'I was eating', वह सो रही थी 'she was sleeping', वे पढ़ रहे थे 'they were studying', लड़कियाँ गा रही थीं 'the girls were singing'. The future continuous uses होगा: वह सो रहा होगा 'he will be / must be sleeping'.

rules.title: Continuous versus habitual
rules.body: The habitual (-ता है) states what someone does generally; the continuous (रहा है) states what is happening right now: मैं हिंदी पढ़ता हूँ 'I study Hindi' versus मैं हिंदी पढ़ रहा हूँ 'I am studying Hindi (at the moment)'. Verbs of knowing, wanting and being usually avoid the continuous: मैं जानता हूँ 'I know', not मैं जान रहा हूँ. The continuous can also refer to the near future: मैं कल जा रहा हूँ 'I am going tomorrow'.

rules.title: The ergative ने with transitive verbs in the past
rules.body: In the perfective tenses (simple past, present perfect, past perfect) the subject of a transitive verb takes ने ne, and the verb agrees with the direct object, not the subject: राम ने किताब पढ़ी rām ne kitāb paṛhī 'Ram read the book' (पढ़ी agrees with f. किताब), लड़की ने खाना खाया 'the girl ate food' (खाया agrees with m. खाना), मैंने चाय पी 'I drank tea'. ने is never used in the present, future, continuous or habitual.

rules.title: ने with pronouns
rules.body: Pronouns take their oblique form before ने and are written together with it: मैंने mainne, तूने tūne, तुमने tumne, हमने hamne, आपने āpne, इसने isne, उसने usne, किसने kisne 'who?', किसी ने kisī ne 'someone'. The plurals are irregular: इन्होंने inhonne, उन्होंने unhonne, किन्होंने. Nouns keep ने separate: राम ने, लड़कों ने.

rules.title: When the object has को, the verb is masculine singular
rules.body: If the direct object is marked with को (or is a को-pronoun like मुझे, उसे), the verb cannot agree with it and takes the default masculine singular form: राम ने लड़की को देखा 'Ram saw the girl' (देखा, not देखी), मैंने उसे बुलाया 'I called her'. The same default applies when there is no object at all: उसने कहा 'he/she said'.

rules.title: Verbs that do not take ने
rules.body: Intransitive verbs (no direct object) never take ने, and the verb agrees with the subject: वह आया, मैं सोई, वे गए. A few verbs with objects also refuse ने: लाना lānā 'bring' (वह किताब लाया), भूलना bhūlnā 'forget' (मैं भूल गया), and बोलना bolnā 'speak' usually does not (वह बोला). Conversely, some verbs that look intransitive in English take ने because they are transitive in Hindi: समझना 'understand' (मैंने समझा), and छींकना 'sneeze' (उसने छींका).

rules.title: Perfect tenses keep ने and object agreement
rules.body: ने also appears in the present perfect and past perfect of transitive verbs, and the participle and auxiliary both agree with the object: मैंने खाना खाया है 'I have eaten', उसने चिट्ठी लिखी थी 'he had written a letter', हमने किताबें पढ़ी हैं 'we have read the books' (f. pl.: पढ़ी + हैं). Questions and negatives are formed as usual: क्या आपने देखा? 'Did you see?', मैंने नहीं खाया 'I didn't eat'.

examples.en: He / she had written a letter.

examples.target: क्या आपने यह फ़िल्म देखी है?
examples.roman: kyā āpne yah film dekhī hai?

rules.title: Object agreement in detail
rules.body: The verb copies the gender and number of the unmarked object: m. sg. -ā (मैंने केला खाया), m. pl. -e (मैंने केले खाए), f. sg. -ī (उसने रोटी खाई), f. pl. -īn (उसने रोटियाँ खाईं, उसने किताबें पढ़ीं). With an auxiliary the nasal moves to the auxiliary: किताबें पढ़ी हैं / पढ़ी थीं. The subject's gender plays no role at all here.

exercises.q: मैं खाना खा ___ हूँ। (I am eating; a man speaking)
exercises.explain: रहा is the masculine singular continuous marker.

exercises.q: वह जा ___ है। (she is going)
exercises.explain: रही is the feminine form.

exercises.q: The continuous is built from the verb stem + रहा/रही/रहे + a form of होना.
exercises.explain: खा रहा हूँ, जा रही है, पढ़ रहे हैं.

exercises.q: बच्चे खेल ___ हैं। (are playing)
exercises.explain: बच्चे is masculine plural, so रहे.

exercises.q: The ergative marker ने is used
options: with transitive verbs in the perfective (past) tenses
with every verb in the past
with transitive verbs in every tense
exercises.explain: ने appears only with transitive verbs in the simple past and perfect tenses.

exercises.q: राम ___ किताब पढ़ी। (ergative marker)
exercises.explain: पढ़ना is transitive and the tense is past, so the subject takes ने.

exercises.q: In राम ने किताब पढ़ी, the verb agrees with किताब (feminine), not with Ram.
exercises.explain: With ने the verb agrees with the unmarked direct object.

exercises.q: The ने form of मैं is
exercises.explain: मैं + ने is written मैंने; मुझे is the को-form.

exercises.q: मैंने चाय ___। (drank; चाय is feminine)
exercises.explain: The verb agrees with the feminine object: पी, not पिया.

exercises.q: वह आया takes ने because the verb is in the past.
exercises.explain: आना is intransitive, so there is no ने: वह आया.

exercises.q: मैंने उसे ___। (I saw him/her; object marked with को-form)
exercises.explain: When the object has को, the verb takes the default masculine singular.

exercises.q: उसने दो किताबें ___। (read; feminine plural object, no auxiliary)
exercises.explain: Feminine plural object gives -ीं on the verb.

exercises.q: वह किताब लाया (he brought the book) is correct without ने because लाना does not take ने.
exercises.explain: लाना, भूलना and usually बोलना are exceptions to the ने rule.

exercises.q: Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explain: जाना is intransitive, so no ने and the verb agrees with the subject.

exercises.answer: क्या आपने यह फ़िल्म देखी है?

exercises.q: वे पढ़ ___ थे। (were studying; masculine plural)
exercises.explain: Past continuous: stem + रहे + थे.

exercises.q: उसने कहा has a masculine singular verb because
options: there is no object for the verb to agree with
ने always makes the verb masculine
exercises.explain: With no unmarked object, the verb takes the default form.

exercises.q: मैं जान रहा हूँ is the normal way to say 'I know'.
exercises.explain: जानना is a stative verb and uses the habitual: मैं जानता हूँ.

exercises.q: ___ केले खाए। (we + ने: 'we ate bananas')
exercises.explain: हम + ने is written हमने.

exercises.q: In मैंने केले खाए, the verb is खाए because
options: the verb always ends in -ए after ने
exercises.explain: The verb agrees with the object केले (m. pl.).

exercises.q: Continuous forms combine with था/थी/थे for the past: वह खा रहा था.
exercises.explain: The past continuous just swaps the auxiliary.

exercises.q: किसने यह किया? means
options: Whom did he do it to?
exercises.explain: किसने is कौन + ने, the subject of a past transitive verb.

sections.title: Questions and negation
sections.summary: Yes/no questions start with क्या, question words sit just before the verb, and Hindi has three negatives: नहीं for statements, मत for commands and न for softer or subjunctive uses. This chapter also covers tag questions and negative words like कोई नहीं.

rules.title: Yes/no questions with क्या
rules.body: A statement becomes a yes/no question by putting क्या kyā at the start; the word order does not change: आप हिंदी बोलते हैं 'you speak Hindi' → क्या आप हिंदी बोलते हैं? 'Do you speak Hindi?'. In speech the क्या is often dropped and rising intonation alone marks the question: आप हिंदी बोलते हैं?

rules.title: क्या as 'what' inside the sentence
rules.body: When क्या stands where the answer would go, usually just before the verb, it means 'what': यह क्या है? 'What is this?', आप क्या करते हैं? 'What do you do?'. Compare क्या यह किताब है? 'Is this a book?' (yes/no) with यह क्या है? 'What is this?'. Position decides the meaning.

rules.title: The question words
rules.body: Hindi question words begin with k-: कौन kaun 'who', क्या kyā 'what', कब kab 'when', कहाँ kahān 'where', किधर kidhar 'which way', क्यों kyon 'why', कैसे kaise 'how (in what way)', कैसा kaisā 'how, of what kind', कितना kitnā 'how much / many', कौन सा kaun sā 'which'. They normally stay in the position of the word they ask about, usually right before the verb, not at the start of the sentence.

rules.title: Question words that agree: कैसा, कितना, कौन सा
rules.body: कैसा, कितना and कौन सा end in -ā and agree like adjectives: आप कैसे हैं? (to a man) / आप कैसी हैं? (to a woman); कितने लोग? 'how many people?', कितनी किताबें? 'how many books?', कितना पानी? 'how much water?'; कौन सी किताब? 'which book?'. कैसे (invariable adverb) means 'how, by what means': आप कैसे आए? 'How did you come?'.

rules.title: Answering: हाँ, नहीं and जी
rules.body: 'Yes' is हाँ hān, 'no' is नहीं nahīn. Adding जी makes both polite: जी हाँ jī hān, जी नहीं jī nahīn. जी alone is a polite 'yes?' or 'yes, sir/madam'. A short answer repeats the verb: क्या आप आएँगे? - हाँ, आऊँगा. 'OK' is ठीक है ṭhīk hai, and अच्छा achchhā means 'I see / all right'.

rules.title: नहीं: the ordinary negative
rules.body: नहीं negates statements and goes right before the verb: मैं नहीं जाता 'I don't go', वह घर पर नहीं है 'he is not at home', मैंने नहीं खाया 'I didn't eat', वह नहीं आएगा 'he won't come'. In the negative habitual the present auxiliary is usually dropped (मैं नहीं जाता rather than मैं नहीं जाता हूँ); with the continuous it is often kept: वह नहीं आ रहा है / वह नहीं आ रहा.

rules.title: न: softer negation, neither...nor, and tags
rules.body: न na is used with the subjunctive and in polite suggestions (आप आज न जाएँ 'please don't go today'), in न... न 'neither... nor' (न चाय न कॉफ़ी), and as a tag at the end of a sentence meaning 'isn't it?' / 'right?': अच्छा है न? 'It's good, isn't it?'. Spoken Hindi often uses ना for the tag. न is softer than मत.

examples.en: This film is good, isn't it?

rules.title: मत: don't (with commands)
rules.body: Prohibitions with the तू and तुम imperatives use मत mat before the verb: मत जाओ 'don't go', यह मत करो 'don't do this', मत रो 'don't cry'. With the polite आप imperative, either मत or न is used: मत कीजिए / न कीजिए 'please don't do it'; न sounds gentler. नहीं is not used with imperatives.

rules.title: Negative words and the double negative
rules.body: 'Nobody', 'nothing', 'never', 'nowhere' are made from the indefinites plus नहीं, and the नहीं is required: कोई नहीं koī nahīn 'no one', कुछ नहीं kuchh nahīn 'nothing', कभी नहीं kabhī nahīn 'never', कहीं नहीं kahīn nahīn 'nowhere'. In a sentence the negative is on the verb: मैं कुछ नहीं जानता 'I don't know anything', कोई नहीं आया 'nobody came', वह कभी नहीं आता 'he never comes'.

rules.title: Negative questions
rules.body: A negative question keeps नहीं before the verb and takes क्या or a question word as usual: क्या वह घर पर नहीं है? 'Isn't he at home?', आप क्यों नहीं आए? 'Why didn't you come?'. Beware: a 'yes' answer agrees with the facts, not with the negative, so हाँ to क्या वह नहीं आया? means 'yes, (it is true that) he didn't come'.

examples.target: क्या वह घर पर नहीं है?
examples.roman: kyā vah ghar par nahīn hai?

exercises.q: To turn आप हिंदी बोलते हैं into a yes/no question, you
exercises.explain: क्या at the start marks a yes/no question without changing the word order.

exercises.q: The word for 'where' is
exercises.explain: कहाँ = where, कब = when, कौन = who, क्यों = why.

exercises.q: क्या at the very beginning of a sentence usually means 'what'.
exercises.explain: Sentence-initial क्या is the yes/no marker; 'what' is क्या placed before the verb.

exercises.q: ___ आप चाय पीते हैं? (yes/no question marker)
exercises.explain: क्या at the start asks 'Do you drink tea?'.

exercises.q: यह क्या है? means
exercises.explain: क्या before the verb is 'what'.

exercises.q: मैं हिंदी ___ बोलता। (not)
exercises.explain: नहीं negates statements and sits before the verb.

exercises.q: नहीं normally comes right before the verb.
exercises.explain: मैं वहाँ नहीं जाता, वह घर पर नहीं है.

exercises.q: The negative command to a friend (तुम) is
exercises.explain: Commands are negated with मत, not नहीं.

exercises.q: यहाँ ___ बैठो। (don't)
exercises.explain: मत + imperative = don't.

exercises.q: मैं कुछ नहीं जानता (I don't know anything) uses a double negative, which is correct Hindi.
exercises.explain: Indefinites like कुछ, कोई, कभी require नहीं on the verb.

exercises.q: आप ___ हैं? (How are you? asking a man)
exercises.explain: कैसा agrees with आप (plural): कैसे for a man, कैसी for a woman.

exercises.q: ___ नहीं आया। (nobody)
exercises.explain: 'Nobody' is कोई + नहीं.

exercises.q: न चाय न कॉफ़ी means
exercises.explain: न... न is 'neither... nor'.

exercises.q: जी हाँ is a polite 'yes'.
exercises.explain: जी makes हाँ and नहीं polite.

exercises.answer: क्या वह घर पर नहीं है?

exercises.q: यह फ़िल्म अच्छी है, ___? (tag: isn't it)
exercises.explain: न (spoken ना) at the end asks for agreement.

exercises.q: वह कभी नहीं आता means
exercises.explain: कभी नहीं = never.

exercises.q: With आप, a polite prohibition can be आप न जाइए or आप मत जाइए.
exercises.explain: Both मत and न work with the -इए imperative; न is gentler.

exercises.q: 'How many books?' is
exercises.explain: कितना agrees with feminine plural किताबें: कितनी.

exercises.q: तुम ___ नहीं आए? (why)
exercises.explain: क्यों 'why' sits before the negative and the verb.

exercises.q: A yes/no question can be made with rising intonation alone, without क्या.
exercises.explain: आप हिंदी बोलते हैं? with rising tone is a question in speech.

exercises.q: Which word order is standard?
exercises.explain: नहीं sits immediately before the verb.

sections.title: Numbers, time and everyday patterns
sections.summary: Hindi numbers up to 100 are each their own word, time is told with बजे and fractions like साढ़े, and many everyday ideas (liking, needing, knowing) put the person in the को-form. This chapter ends with the basics of compound verbs.

rules.title: Numbers 1 to 10
rules.body: एक ek 1, दो do 2, तीन tīn 3, चार chār 4, पाँच pānch 5, छह chhah 6 (also written छः), सात sāt 7, आठ āṭh 8, नौ nau 9, दस das 10. Zero is शून्य śūnya or ज़ीरो. After a number the noun is plural: दो किताबें 'two books', तीन लड़के 'three boys', पाँच कमरे; 'people' is लोग: चार लोग.

rules.title: 11 to 100: every number is its own word
rules.body: Hindi does not build 'twenty-three' from parts; each number to 99 is a separate word to memorise. 11-20: ग्यारह gyārah, बारह bārah, तेरह terah, चौदह chaudah, पंद्रह pandrah, सोलह solah, सत्रह satrah, अठारह aṭhārah, उन्नीस unnīs, बीस bīs. Tens: तीस tīs 30, चालीस chālīs 40, पचास pachās 50, साठ sāṭh 60, सत्तर sattar 70, अस्सी assī 80, नब्बे nabbe 90, सौ sau 100. Numbers ending in 9 are 'one less than' the next ten: उन्नीस 19, उनतीस untīs 29, उनचास unchās 49.

rules.title: Large numbers and ordinals
rules.body: Above a hundred Hindi counts in हज़ार hazār 'thousand', लाख lākh 'hundred thousand' and करोड़ karoṛ 'ten million': एक लाख = 100,000; दस लाख = a million; एक करोड़ = 10,000,000. Ordinals: पहला pahlā 'first', दूसरा dūsrā 'second', तीसरा tīsrā 'third', चौथा chauthā 'fourth', then number + -वाँ: पाँचवाँ pānchvān 'fifth', छठा chhaṭhā 'sixth', दसवाँ 'tenth'. They agree like -ā adjectives: पहली बार 'the first time'.

rules.title: Halves and quarters
rules.body: आधा ādhā 'half', डेढ़ ḍeṛh 'one and a half', ढाई ḍhāī 'two and a half', and from three on साढ़े sāṛhe + number 'n and a half': साढ़े तीन 3.5, साढ़े पाँच 5.5. सवा savā + number is 'n and a quarter' (सवा चार 4.25) and पौने paune + number is 'a quarter less than n' (पौने पाँच 4.75). These words are used for time, money and quantities: डेढ़ किलो 'one and a half kilos', ढाई सौ 250.

rules.title: Telling the time with बजे
rules.body: 'O'clock' is बजे baje (from बजना 'to strike'): दो बजे हैं 'it is two o'clock', with one o'clock singular: एक बजा है. Fractions go in front: साढ़े तीन बजे 3:30, सवा चार बजे 4:15, पौने पाँच बजे 4:45, डेढ़ बजे 1:30, ढाई बजे 2:30. Minutes use बजकर: पाँच बजकर दस मिनट 5:10. Ask कितने बजे हैं? 'What time is it?'. 'At five' is also पाँच बजे.

rules.title: Parts of the day and days of the week
rules.body: सुबह subah 'morning', दोपहर dopahar 'afternoon', शाम śām 'evening', रात rāt 'night'; 'in the morning' is just सुबह, 'in the evening' शाम को, 'at night' रात को. Days: सोमवार somvār Monday, मंगलवार mangalvār, बुधवार budhvār, गुरुवार guruvār, शुक्रवार śukravār, शनिवार śanivār, रविवार ravivār Sunday (also इतवार). 'On Monday' is सोमवार को; 'today' आज, 'this week' इस हफ़्ते.

examples.en: We will go to Delhi on Monday.

rules.title: Liking: X को Y पसंद है
rules.body: 'I like tea' is मुझे चाय पसंद है mujhe chāy pasand hai: the person is in the को-form, the liked thing is the subject, and the verb agrees with it: मुझे आम पसंद हैं 'I like mangoes' (plural हैं), उसे हिंदी फ़िल्में पसंद हैं 'she likes Hindi films'. Add बहुत for 'very much' and नहीं for 'don't like': मुझे यह पसंद नहीं है. The past is पसंद था/थी/थे.

examples.target: क्या आपको यह शहर पसंद है?
examples.roman: kyā āpko yah śahar pasand hai?

rules.title: Needing and wanting: चाहिए and चाहना
rules.body: 'I need / want water' is मुझे पानी चाहिए mujhe pānī chāhie, again with the person in the को-form; चाहिए does not change (plural चाहिएँ is optional). With an infinitive it means 'should': मुझे जाना चाहिए 'I should go', आपको आराम करना चाहिए 'you should rest'. The verb चाहना chāhnā 'to want' works with an ordinary subject: मैं चाय चाहता हूँ 'I want tea', मैं जाना चाहती हूँ 'I (f.) want to go'.

rules.title: Compound verbs: लेना, देना, जाना as 'vectors'
rules.body: Hindi often pairs a verb stem with a second 'vector' verb that carries the tense and adds a shade of meaning. लेना suggests the action benefits the doer or is completed: खा लो 'eat up', मैंने कर लिया 'I've done it'. देना suggests it is done for someone else: दे दो 'hand it over', बता दो 'tell (them)'. जाना marks completion or a change of state and is used with intransitives: चला गया 'went away', सो गया 'fell asleep', हो गया 'it's done'. Compounds with जाना never take ने.

rules.title: Everyday patterns with को: लगना, आना, age
rules.body: Many feelings and abilities put the person in the को-form. लगना lagnā 'to seem, to feel': मुझे ठंड लग रही है 'I am feeling cold', मुझे लगता है कि... 'I think that...', यह अच्छा लगता है 'I like this (it seems good to me)'. 'Know (a skill or language)' is आना: मुझे हिंदी आती है 'I know Hindi', उसे तैरना आता है 'he can swim'. Age uses का: मैं बीस साल का हूँ 'I am twenty' (f. बीस साल की).

examples.target: मुझे लगता है कि वह आएगा।
examples.roman: mujhe lagtā hai ki vah āegā.

exercises.q: तीन is
'ten' is
पाँच means five.
exercises.explain: पाँच pānch = 5.

exercises.q: ___ बजे हैं। (it is two o'clock)
exercises.explain: दो बजे हैं = it is two o'clock.

exercises.q: 'It is one o'clock' is
exercises.explain: One o'clock is singular: एक बजा है; from two on, बजे हैं.

exercises.q: मुझे चाय ___ है। (I like tea)
exercises.explain: Liking: person + को, thing, पसंद + होना.

exercises.q: डेढ़ means one and a half.
exercises.explain: डेढ़ 1.5, ढाई 2.5, then साढ़े + number.

exercises.q: साढ़े चार बजे is
exercises.explain: साढ़े + number = half past that hour.

exercises.q: ___ चार बजे (quarter past four, 4:15)
exercises.explain: सवा + number = a quarter past.

exercises.q: मुझे जाना चाहिए means
exercises.explain: को + infinitive + चाहिए expresses 'should'.

exercises.q: The number 19 (one less than बीस) is ___
exercises.explain: Numbers ending in 9 are 'one less than' the next ten: उन्नीस.

exercises.q: उनचास (49) is built as 'one less than fifty'.
exercises.explain: उन- 'one less' + पचास-like stem gives 49.

exercises.q: एक लाख is
exercises.explain: लाख = a hundred thousand; दस लाख = a million.

exercises.q: मैं चाय ___ हूँ। (want; a woman speaking)
exercises.explain: चाहना takes an ordinary subject and agrees with it: feminine चाहती.

exercises.q: The compound खा लो (with लेना) suggests
options: eat it up, for your own benefit
exercises.explain: The vector लेना points the action towards the doer and marks completion.

exercises.q: मुझे हिंदी आती है means 'I know Hindi' (literally 'Hindi comes to me').
exercises.explain: Skills and languages are known with आना and the को-form.

exercises.q: मुझे ठंड लग ___ है। (I am feeling cold; ठंड is feminine)
exercises.explain: The continuous रही agrees with the subject ठंड (f.).

exercises.q: कितने बजे हैं? means
exercises.explain: Literally 'how many have struck?'.

exercises.en: We will go to Delhi on Monday.

exercises.q: After a number, Hindi nouns stay singular: पाँच किताब.
exercises.explain: The noun goes plural: पाँच किताबें.

exercises.q: मुझे ___ है कि वह आएगा। (it seems / I think)
exercises.explain: मुझे लगता है कि... = I think that...

exercises.q: मैं बीस साल का हूँ means
options: I have been here twenty years
exercises.explain: Age is expressed with साल का/की: 'of twenty years'.

exercises.q: ढाई बजे is 2:30.
exercises.explain: ढाई = two and a half, so ढाई बजे = half past two.
